name: Agatu
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Idomoid, presumably tonal; only Armstrong classification notes and Ethnologue found; no phonology/grammar located (Glottolog, OLAC, Crossref all empty).

new_statements.quote: All the other Idomoid languages have three-register systems. Except for the very special case of Yala (Ikom), downdrift is rare and downstep non-existent. [p. 96; 'other' = other than Igede, which 'has a four-level, register tone system'] ... Idoma itself, a cluster of ten dialects strung out from Lafia to Obubra and Ikom ... tonally the cognate forms are at least 98 percent identical in their citation forms [p. 94]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (58-page JWAL scan, no text layer) and rendered pdf pp. 5 and 40 (printed pp. 96 and 131) as images to check the scanned against the page. Printed p. 96, third-from-last paragraph, reads exactly: "In addition, Igede has a four-level, register tone system that seems ancient, since there are no contextual, lexical or grammatical constraints on the occurrence of any of the tones. It would be hard to specify which is the 'fourth' tone. All the other Idomoid languages have three-register systems. Except for the very special case of Yala (Ikom), downdrift is rare and downstep non-existent." Printed p. 94 (pdf p. 3), first paragraph, reads exactly: "Idoma itself, a cluster of ten dialects s…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Agatu is a register tone language with three level tones (high, mid, low); tone, not stress, is the lexically contrastive prosody. No source opened says anything about word stress or accent in Agatu (grep for stress/accent returns nothing in Armstrong 1983, Samuel 2015 or Ogra 2017).
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Agatu-specific corroboration: Samuel, Jerry Idu. 2015. A study of the form, content and performance of Agatu songs. PhD thesis, ABU Zaria, p. 149: "The song is expressed in Agatu, a tonal language which really functions when it is spoken with its proper tone pattern. Despite the fact that its syllables can be indicated by high, mid and low tones, its musical form cannot be satisfactorily rendered in translation." (file). Ogra 2017: 37 (citing Odumuh 1994) gives Idoma a three-level discrete register system H/M/L.
new_statements.domain_note: Armstrong's tone remarks concern citation forms of lexical stems in comparative wordlists (Swadesh 200 list from Rev. Hugh Mackay 1963 and Armstrong's own 1951 elicitation from the Chief of Bagaji); word level, no phrase-level prosody discussed. Nothing on stress at any level.
new_statements.identity_note: Agatu is treated by Armstrong (1983: 94, 131) and by Nigerian Idoma scholarship (Abraham's five varieties; Ogra 2017: 5-6, 49) as the northernmost dialect of the Idoma dialect cluster (Idoma = idom1241), not as a separate language; Ethnologue/Glottolog give it its own code agc / agat1236. The quoted Armstrong statement is made for the Idomoid languages as a group (Idoma cluster incl. Agatu, Igede, Akweya, Eloyi, Etulo), with Agatu itself sketched in his sec. 3.1.3; the Agatu-specific tonal statement (H/M/L) is Samuel 2015: 149, a literature PhD by an Agatu-area scholar, not a phonological description.

sources.citation: Ogra, Owole Comfort. 2017. Contrastive analysis of lexical and phonological variations in Enone and Enochi varieties of Idoma language. MA thesis, Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria. 141 pp.
sources.note: Not about Agatu; nothing on stress. p. 37: Idoma has a three tone-level discrete register system H/M/L (citing Odumuh 1994). pp. 5-6: Agatu is one of Abraham's five Idoma varieties. p. 47: Methodist Mission at Ika studied the Agatu variety in the 1960s (Rev. Hugh Mackay, then Spencer Dibble). p. 48: Akpala 1993 (ABU undergraduate project) covers phonology of Otukpo, Agatu, Edumoga, Akweya, Yache; p. 49 gives Agatu 'oyicho' moon.
